raw_comment:
1. I notice that texting, phone calls, and video chatting increased for all ages, though people ages 15-24 had the highest increase, 8 minutes. I also notice that those ages 15-24 were the only ones to have a decrease in exercising, but they do still exercise the most out of all age groups. In addition,  they were the only age group to have an increase in grooming, albeit 0.4 minutes. However, compared to the decrease the other age groups had, 2. it makes me wonder what's special about this age group. Well, this age group is still going through school or college, and obviously, the elephant in the room, 2020 was the year COVID-19 struck. This means students were doing school virtually, and had more free time. So then, why did exercising decrease? Probably because all public gyms had closed, and most people would be scared to go on walks, because, well, the answer is fairly self-evident. Other age groups might be able to workout in their own home, but probably not college students. Grooming makes sense to me, since college students probably didn't have much time to take care of themselves before the pandemic, so during the pandemic, not too much changed, even a slight increase in how much they groom themselves, while other age groups didn't prioritize it as much.
3. This relates to me and my community since everyone experienced and was impacted by the pandemic, and I identify with these graphs a lot.
4. How did the pandemic change the way we use our free time?

1. What do you notice?

I notice that Texting, phone calls, and video chats all went up for all age groups and to me, this is not surprising at all. raw_comment:
Things are slowly returning to the old normal, but from the graph, we see that some of our own habits remain unchanged from during the pandemic.
The first thing I noticed was the increase in time spent on video chats and messages. What surprised me was that it had not decreased during all this time. It made sense, perhaps during the beginning of the pandemic and quarantine, when regulations were high. Back then, video chats were the only way you could communicate with your friends. But now, most students have gotten their vaccines, and the younger ones who haven’t got them don't need them to see friends. Face-to-face is now common in day-to-day life, and students already spend 6 hours a day interacting with others. After school, they hang out at the park to play basketball. They don’t exactly prefer to video chat with each other; at least, I can’t imagine why they would.
Even though we’re moving away from the secluded society which was the result of coronavirus, we have not changed our habits. Maybe it’s because we’re lazy, maybe it’s because we find that our new habits suit us better. Whatever the reason, we’re changing and developing as a society, making new adaptations as time passes. Perhaps we’ll never go back to the old normal, but instead stay at an ongoing normal.
Headline: Are We as Adaptable as Our Environment?

raw_comment: I notice that the 15-24 age group's time on their cellphones increased more than all of the other groups. We went from spending the second most time on our phones out of all the age groups to being the group who spent the most time on our phones. I also notice that the 15-24 year olds actually increased their grooming time by a little. I think this is because we spent the pandemic experimenting with the way we do our hair, how we dress, and the way we do our makeup. I wonder in the first graph why the 65+ group was using their cell phones to call and text more than the 15-24 age group when they are often the ones who say that we use our phones too much. This relates to me in the sense that most of the data for my age group accurately represents what happened with me. I started using my phone to text and call more, and I started to spend a little more time on my hair, makeup, and skin care. The middle graph however, is not accurate for me because the amount of exercise I get never changed. A good title for this graph would be the pandemic, where all of our screen time increased, people 25 and up started exercising more, and every generation except for Gen Z stopped caring about their looks.

1. **Chart type**  
   Multi-series **line chart**, shown as three separate panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Small multiples / faceting** by activity type:
     - Texting, phone calls and video chats
     - Exercising
     - Grooming
   - Each panel contains multiple colored lines for **age groups**.
   - No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Activity type (Texting/phone calls/video chats, Exercising, Grooming) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting / separate panels |
| Year (2019, 2020) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Average non-work and non-school time spent per day (minutes per day) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Age group (15–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+) | Categorical/ordinal | Color/hue of lines and points |
| Change from 2019 to 2020 (e.g., +8 min., −5 min.) | Quantitative | Text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
1. The graphs are of average free time spent per day by age. They show the difference in minutes from 2019 to 2020. The four age groups are 15-24, 25-44, 45-64, and 65+. For all age groups time spent texting, phone calls, and videos calls increased. For ages 15-24 time spent exercising decreased by five minutes, but for the other groups it increased by 4 or 5 minutes. Grooming decreased for all groups except 15-24, which had a small increase. 

2. I wonder why the time spent texting and on phone and video calls is so low. From my experience and observation people spend much longer than 15 minutes a day texting or on calls. Maybe the number is so low because it only counts communication and not social media. I also wonder why ages 15-24 exercised less. Being at home more seems to have affected exercise time of very young people differently than everyone else, according to this graph. I also wonder why ages 15-24 spent slightly more time grooming. This could be because people those ages still had to be on video calls or even in person for school, so they still maintained their appearances.

3. This impacts my community because the pandemic did affect how we spend our time. For my community the increase in time spent texting and on calls and decrease in time exercising generally applies. The almost no change in time spent grooming also makes sense because we still had to go to school.

4. “The Pandemic Redistributes Our Free Time”

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I noticed that texting, phone calls, and video chats increased the most for 15-24 year-olds and also increased in every other age group. This is because everyone was communicating by phone or video chat during quarantine. Everyone spent less time grooming because they didn’t have anywhere to be. I also noticed that 15-24 year olds were the only ones who reported a little change in time spent grooming. 

What do you wonder? 
I am curious as to why it says that 15-24 years olds are only on their phones for 15 minutes a day in this report, being 17 years old myself I can say with confidence that many people my age are spending hours on their phones, especially during quarantine. I am also curious as to why 15-24 year olds didn’t have as drastic of a decrease in time spent grooming than the other ages.


How does this relate to your community?
There were a lot of people in my community who spent time on their phones or spent time video chatting, however, a lot of my friends and family also spent the time doing exercises. My family, whom most would fit in the older category, would have fit in with what the graph shows us, I definitely would not.

What do you notice? 

I notice that my age group (15-24) increased in online communication by significantly more time than other age groups. Also, my age group has decreased in exercise whereas every other age group has increased in that area. Lastly, my age group was the only group to increase in grooming, which shows how we're dedicating more time to self-care, at least in that arena. 

What do you wonder? 

I wonder why my age group increased in grooming yet decreased in exercise, as self-care usually includes both grooming and exercise -- these two factors are usually linked. Furthermore, I wonder why other age groups decreased in grooming, perhaps because they had to work even more at home whereas school time is typically constant. 

How does this relate to you and your community? 

It's interesting to see how my age group, late teens and early adults, have an increased electronics use and on the whole, are dedicating less time to self-care despite the greater amount of free time due to less homework and fewer commitments (on average). Furthermore, I feel like other age groups are more readily able to purchase goods/services, which may have led to the increase in exercise (for instance, they can buy a Peloton bike) amongst other age groups. The changes in grooming amongst other groups make sense because they don't need to look as good for work at home, but grooming in our age group is still a mystery to me. 

Catchy headline: Gen Z is truly the digital generation.

raw_comment: This graph depicts the trend of certain activities in certain age groups in 2019 and 2020. I think that Covid-19 is a huge factor in many of the results. In all age groups, texting, phone calls, and video chats all increased. This is because of the lack of in-person communication that everyone had access to during quarantine. For all age groups except 15-24, exercise increased likely due to an increase in free time. For teens and young adults, however, exercising decreased. I believe this is because the use of electronic communication increased drastically more than any other group and almost replaced exercising all together. Grooming decreased in every age group except for 15-24, which honestly surprised me and I'm curious as to why this is. This relates to my life and community because as someone in the 15-24 age group, my phone usage has certainly followed the trend shown on the graph and it is a habit I'm trying to break. My title for this graph is "The Pandemic's Affect on Each Age Group's Time Usage"

|---|---|---|

raw_comment: In the first graph, I notice that texting, phone calls, and video chats for all 4 groups increased, the 15-24 group increasing the most by 8 minutes. In the second graph, the 15-24 group was the only group that decreased their amount of time spent exercising while the other 3 groups increased. In the last graph, the 15-24 group was an outlier again, being the only group that increased their grooming time. The three other groups decreased substantially more. It's clear that the 15-24 group had very different results compared to the older groups. I wonder why the 15-24 group decreased their exercise over the last year while the older groups increased. Another question that relates to exercising is why the 15-24 group groomed themselves more while the older groups groomed less. It's an odd mix of the amount of self-care, decreasing exercise while increasing their grooming. These graphs relate to me and my community because everyone around me, including myself, has changed over the last year because of the pandemic. Using technology to communicate increased for everyone due to clear reasons like social distancing and attempting to stop the spread of COVID. Self-care over the past year differs for everyone I know. Some people have taken the time to rebuild themselves by working out or learning new things, while others struggled more mentally, causing them to not be as productive. A headline for this graph would be "Comparing the Use of Free Time with Each Generation"

1. I notice that time spent on technology was the only category where everyone's time increased. 

2. - It's stressed that young people exercise a lot to stay healthy, so why aren't they exercising much during the pandemic? Is it because their only options are outdoor and outside activities? But then why wouldn't that have an effect on those older than them?

3. My community was already very online-centric, and this fact was only exasperated as the pandemic rolled in. This experience is similar to the left-most graph, where an already-online-related community only became more dependent on technology during the pandemic. 

4. Because of the pandemic, people of all ages spend more time using technology. Those who are ages 18-24 spend more of their time grooming, while also spending less on exercising; this development is most likely due to them needing to sacrifice *some* time for other unmentioned jobs. However, the times people of ages 25+ spent on grooming and exercising have undergone the opposite effects respectively. This increase in exercising is most likely due to the elderly needing to keep in shape, and the fact that 25 is not an old age whatsover; this once again leads to some of their time needing to be sacrificed, and grooming seems to be one of them. 
Title: "The Permanent Effects of the Pandemic on our Leisure Time"

raw_comment:
1) All three graphs above depict similar results in that the age group is always the outlier. For example, in the first graph all of the age groups increased their time spent on their phones only by two to three minutes. Whereas the 15-24 age group increased their time spent on their phones by a whopping eight minutes. Although an increase in 8 minutes may not sound like much, comparatively speaking (with respect to the other age groups) it is a huge increase.  
2) Throughout the pandemic, technology because everyone's primary source of communication, work, etc. - so it is not unexpected that there would be an increase across the board of technology use. However, since everyone was using technology for everything it seemed like, I wonder why only the one age group increased by such a great amount. 
3) The information relates to my community and me because, throughout the pandemic, I noticed myself going on my phone and computer much more than I would have if things were normal. However, I also noticed that my parents were doing the same as well. This causes me to think: "If everyone was using technology for everything now, how is it that only my age group increased?" After thinking about this question, the results made sense. Although it is a bad habit, I feel that my age group was more likely to go on their phones while we were in online school whereas our parents, were focused on their work. 
4) How Different Generations Spent Their Time Before vs After the Pandemic

raw_comment:
1) From these graphs, I noticed that the 15-24 age group had an 8-minute increase in texting, phone call, and video chat usage, but a 5-minute decrease in exercising. The two could be correlated, as people could be spending more time on their electronics, and less time being physically active. However, it was honestly surprising to see a 0.4-minute increase in time spent grooming, which does make sense, considering the greater amount of time on our hands.
2) Personally, I wonder why the 25-44, 45-64, and 65+ age groups experienced a pretty large decline in time spent grooming, but an increase in exercising. While grooming and exercising are both very necessary to personal health, I'd assume basic hygiene would be more of a priority.
3) As a person who falls between the 15-24 age group, the statistics specific to my age group relate to my own experience during quarantine. Being a remote student last year, I definitely spent more time texting and calling my friends, since we couldn't interact in-person as frequently. It was also difficult to motivate myself to go on runs, as I would regularly do during track or cross-country in previous years, but I still tried to go on walks a few times a week.
4) "Daily Life During the Pandemic: A New Age of Habit" - This headline refers to the various daily habits that have changed during the pandemic, with the relevant keywords "age" and "habit".

raw_comment:
Most striking in these graphs is the large contrast between those of age 15-24 and those aged 25+.  For example, while phone usage has increased for all age groups, younger populations are being much more dramatically affected by the onset of the pandemic.

The difference is much more noticeable in the other two graphs; while older age groups are rising in exercise time and lowering time dedicated to grooming, younger populations are experiencing lower levels of exercising and higher levels of grooming.

The age group highlighted in yellow is mostly delegated to students in high school and college. Thus, there is a large factor that creates a pandemic experience dramatically different than adults.

I wonder what pressures during the pandemic are being placed on students that compel them to overperform. They are spending more time glued to their phones and less time exercising. Moreover, an increase in grooming time implies that they are still expected to look fashionable to their online peers. What tasks are they doing on their phones that drains so much of their time?

As a high schooler, I witness the physical and mental deterioration of my fellow classmates, and understanding this data could be crucial for improving the mental health of students that are experiencing increasing levels of stress during the pandemic. 

Thus, my catchy headline: Student populations are placed under unrealistic expectations for increased online presence, draining their time and mental health.

raw_comment:
1) The 15-24 age group tended to stand out from the other populations somehow, with phone time increasing more dramatically, exercise decreasing where for others it decreased, and grooming increasing (if only marginally) where for others it decreased dramatically. Some of these make sense - younger generations might be more technologically up-to-date or more used to phone usage as part of normal life, and classes might interfere with time to go to the gym.

2) I do not understand why grooming increased/stayed the same, especially when all other age groups' habits decreased so dramatically. If anything, I would think that grooming would decrease, since classes were primarily virtual.

3) Increased time on the Internet and exposures to all different types of content can be debilitating for many adolescents' upbringing. In addition, increased screen time as a habit itself might affect work ethic, attention span, etc.

4) "Routine Disturbance: Pandemic Habits Across Age Groups." This title can be read two ways, since "routine" is both an adjective and a noun, and therefore describes both dramatic shifts, or disturbances, in previous lifestyles, and regular, reoccuring disturbance in the present pandemic lifestyle. While over time these changes are observable and obvious, in the moment, they are just another part of life; the "new normal" was a lack of any form of normallity.

raw_comment:
The graphs depict how people from different age groups spent their free time during the pandemic. The data tracks three main categories: communication via phones, exercising, and grooming.

Throughout the three data sets, there has been one common trend. The graphs for the age groups of 25 and older tend to mirror each other in a linear manner, while the graph for people aged 15-24 typically followed a different pattern.

For example, the exercising chart shows that while people from the ages of 25 and up slightly increased the amount they exercise on a day-to-day basis, people below that age mark decreased their physical activity.

This data set is  applicable to me and my community, simply because almost everybody I know falls under the surveyed age groups. It can be used to analyze potential trends in the future about health concerns, technology proficiency, and other factors that have changed as a result of the pandemic.

I'm curious about other potential categories.

raw_comment:
I notice that the four age groups differ in their average non-work and non-school time spent per day, and that all four age groups have been drastically affected by some factor (presumably the Covid pandemic). As a 17 year old, I notice the changes in the 15-24 age group the most: increased time spent texting/calling/video chatting, decreased time exercising, and a slight change in time spent grooming (whereas the other age groups have spent much less time grooming). While the other three age groups tend to move in a similar fashion, 15-24 year olds seem to be a bit more "independent".

I wonder how these statistics were gathered. What is the sample size and was the data collected from a representative population reflective of the country? Probably the most striking statistic is the increase in grooming time for 15-24 year olds, while an opposite change can be observed in the other age groups. Why is this? For the second graph, does the data take into account mandatory virtual PE classes?

Obviously, these statistics are very relevant to all people in the US, whose school and work have been affected by the pandemic. The first graph resonates well with my own personal experiences, as my friends and I have spent much more time video chatting compared to 2019.

1. I noticed that the younger generation (15-24), increased screen time/ technology usage during the pandemic. This is related to the isolation period- where I can imagine all teenagers and young adults spent their time hours on a screen. Exercising increased for the older generation as they had more time to do remote work. As for grooming, the younger generation enjoyed it while the older generation was less focused on it.

Whether it was a phone call, zoom call, or social media, communication was the glue that held us together through this pandemic. Though it was interesting for me to see the difference in technology from the older generation. It makes me think about what hobbies they’ve done throughout this time.

raw_comment:
Did We Change For The Better Or For The Worst? 

I notice that for every age group, the time spent on texting, phone calls, and video chats increased over the course of the pandemic. The exercise results vary; people of younger ages, 15-24, decreased their exercise whereas the adults, ages 45+ increased their exercise. For the most part, grooming decreased. I wonder if this is all due to the pandemic. I also wonder if students decreased their exercise due to mental health reasons and/or being outside of school, where there is no physical education provided to them. As for the older ages, I wonder if they exercised more because most were working from home and had more free time. I wonder if people exercised because they wanted to better themselves or maybe for weight loss. I wonder if the use of technology increased because most of the population had an increase in spare time and time spent at home. Finally, I wonder if the decrease in grooming occurred because there was an increase in isolation amongst the community. As previously stated, this all relates back to the community because, at the times of May through December 2020, a worldwide pandemic occurred where everyone was forced to quarantine. Overall, the graph is displaying the changes in how we spend our free time before and during the pandemic.

raw_comment: Today, this graph is displaying the average amount of time different age groups spent doing a variety activities in 2019 vs. 2020. The categories: texting, phone calls and video chats, exercising, and grooming. For the first category, every age groups minutes spent using their phone increased from 2019 until 2020, some as much as an 8 min increase. This can be attributed to one factor: COVID-19 pandemic. With kids and adults staying home all day, it's easier to find time to text, play games, etc. Also, without having the constant contact with peers in the workplace or school, people had to communicate through the internet with texting and calling. The next graph shows a decrease and increase in exercise from 2019 to 2020. The 15-24 year olds had a steady decline starting at 35 minutes of exercise a day, and ending with only 30. Given that with everyone being home you should have more free time, this statistic can only be attributed to the people actually wanting to exercise. Things like gym class and sports sort of forced exercise on this age category, and without it people chose not to exercise. The 25-44 and 65+ categories actually had a steady increase of 4 more minutes of exercise a day. The opposite occurred here, so when given more time, 25 to 65 year olds use it to exercise. The last statistic is a scary one...for since people were not leaving the house, it appears as if the time spent grooming was shortened entirely except for the 15-24 who barely spent more time.

1.I noticed that the use of technology increased in every age group. This is not surprising to me because of how the pandemic has affected our day to day lives. I also noticed that the amount of exercise received decreased in the age group of 15-24, but had increased in all of the other groups. What do you notice?

I notice how the younger generation increased their use of technology while isolated during the pandemic. At the same time exercising was less accessible for the younger age group (probably due to the decrease in sports and group activities) while the older generation had more time to exercise with remote work. Finally the younger generation spent more time grooming while the older generation decided it was less fruitful.

What do you wonder?

I wonder the impact of social media on the actions of the 15-24 year old age group. For instance, grooming could have increased due to the prevalence of a younger beauty standard proliferated by social media. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

The majority of my community fall into the youngest age group, and many of the trends can be seen through overall sentiments I have seen. This also relates to a family dynamic which is part of my community. As the older generation engages in hobbies away from technology (for my family hiking), the young became more immersed in it.

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.

The generational pandemic.

Title: How did society's habits change during the pandemic?

In the first graph, the use of electronics including texting, phone calls and video chats increase significantly amongst all age groups compared from 2019 to 2020. In the second graph, the amount of exercise of individuals ages 15-24 decreased versus the slight increase in other age groups. In the last graph, people aged 45-64 decrease grooming significantly along with those aged 25-44 and 65+. People aged 15-24 saw no change. 

These three graphs document the habits of four different age groups before and during the pandemic. While younger people responded better to technology and communication devices, they did not respond as well to exercise but kept their grooming habits.   Other age groups did not respond as well to technology and struggled to maintain their grooming habits, but kept up their exercise regimen. 

I wonder why exercise decreased for younger people, considering they're the most physically abled group of people.

I wonder why the three older age groups stayed relatively the same, although there is a 40 year difference and the statistics stayed very similar for all three.

In the last graph, ages 25+ had a decrease in grooming while the only age group to have an increase in grooming were ages 15-24. This graph could be called Body Over Mind.

Our daily live's being changed by the pandemic

I noticed how the pandemic changed so much in our daily lives, not only on big things like traveling or going to school daily but also, on normal simple things like exercising, taking care of ourselves and the time we spend in front of screens.    Multi-series **line chart**, shown as three separate panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Small multiples / faceting** by activity type:
     - Texting, phone calls and video chats
     - Exercising
     - Grooming
   - Each panel contains multiple colored lines for **age groups**.
   - No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Activity type (Texting/phone calls/video chats, Exercising, Grooming) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting / separate panels |
| Year (2019, 2020) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Average non-work and non-school time spent per day (minutes per day) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Age group (15–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+) | Categorical/ordinal | Color/hue of lines and points |
| Change from 2019 to 2020 (e.g., +8 min., −5 min.) | Quantitative | Text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
Time Spent doing Activities in People According to 
 Age Group

This graph appears to show nonwork and school time activities from 2019 to 2020. The 3 categories are texting, phone calls, and video chats. exercising, and grooming. The ages involved in this graph are 15-24, 25-44, 45-64, and 65+ year olds. Something I notice is the trends are different for each age group. Use of electronics and exercising went up for each age group, however exercising went down for the age group 15-24. Also for grooming each age group went down, except age group 15-24 went up a little. One thing I'm wondering is why the data doesn't begin at the bottom of the graph. I think this relates to my community and I because it shows 2019, which was life pre-Covid and then 2020 during Covid. A lot of people's lives changed a lot during this time, so it's interesting to see the different changes in activity.
